items.prompt: What is a feature flag, as this unit defines it?
choices: A runtime switch, checked with an if at the point new behavior would run, that decides whether that code executes
A git tag marking a release version
A comment in code marking a TODO
A special branch name that triggers automatic deployment
items.explanation: A feature flag is a runtime decision point (usually a boolean or percentage), not a git construct — it lets code exist in main without being exposed to users yet.
items.reference:
Feature flag
a runtime switch (usually boolean or %) checked with an if
separates merging code from releasing a feature

Why: Merging becomes a safe git event; releasing becomes a reversible config change.

items.prompt: What's the key distinction a feature flag creates that a long-lived branch doesn't?
choices: It separates merging code (safe, cheap) from releasing a feature (risky, reversible if planned)
It makes code review unnecessary
It guarantees the code has zero bugs before merging
It replaces the need for automated tests
items.explanation: The core value of a flag is decoupling two events that a long-lived branch conflates: getting code into main, and exposing it to real users.
items.reference:
Feature flag
a runtime switch (usually boolean or %) checked with an if
separates merging code from releasing a feature

Why: Merging becomes a safe git event; releasing becomes a reversible config change.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what specifically made the team afraid to merge the 9-day checkout PR?
choices: Merging it would have shipped an untested confirmation screen to every customer at once, since merging and releasing were the same event
The PR had a typo in its title
GitHub was down that week
The branch had too few commits to review properly
items.explanation: Without a flag, merge and release are the same moment — so a big, partly-untested change merging means it goes live for everyone simultaneously.
items.reference:
Feature flag
a runtime switch (usually boolean or %) checked with an if
separates merging code from releasing a feature

Why: Merging becomes a safe git event; releasing becomes a reversible config change.

items.prompt: What does trunk-based development mean, as this unit uses the term?
choices: Committing small, working changes directly to main (or merging within hours) multiple times a day, keeping main always releasable
Never creating any git branch, ever, under any circumstance
Deploying to production automatically on every single commit with no review
Keeping one long-lived branch per developer that merges once a quarter
items.explanation: Trunk-based development is about branch lifetime and merge frequency — small changes landing on main constantly — not about eliminating branches or review entirely.
items.reference:
Trunk-based development
everyone commits small changes to main multiple times a day
main stays always releasable

Why: Short-lived work avoids the drift that turned the checkout PR into 11 conflicts by day 9.

items.prompt: Why did the 9-day checkout branch accumulate 11 conflicts by day 9 but had 0 on day 1?
choices: The longer the branch stayed unmerged, the further main drifted from the commit it branched from, making reconciliation harder every day
Conflicts are assigned randomly by git regardless of branch age
The developer made a mistake in the first commit
GitHub counts conflicts differently after 5 days
items.explanation: Conflict growth here is a direct function of branch age: every day main moves forward without the branch, more of that divergence has to be reconciled at merge time.
items.reference:
Trunk-based development
everyone commits small changes to main multiple times a day
main stays always releasable

Why: Short-lived work avoids the drift that turned the checkout PR into 11 conflicts by day 9.

items.prompt: An on-call engineer needs to instantly disable a risky code path in production without doing a deploy. Which flag type is this?
choices: An ops toggle / kill switch
A release toggle
An experiment flag
A permission toggle
items.explanation: An ops toggle (kill switch) exists specifically for instant, deploy-free disabling of a risky path — exactly the Day 3 incident in L3's scenario.
items.reference:
Flag types
release toggle — hides unfinished work, temporary
ops/kill switch — instant production disable
experiment flag — A/B routing
permission toggle — plan/role gating, often long-term

Why: Different flag types have different expected lifespans — release toggles should be removed; permission toggles often shouldn't.

items.prompt: A team wants to route 10% of users to a new pricing page design to measure conversion differences. Which flag type is this?
choices: An experiment flag (A/B test)
A release toggle
An ops toggle / kill switch
A permission toggle
items.explanation: Routing a percentage of traffic to measure an effect is exactly what an experiment flag is for, distinct from a release toggle's goal of safely rolling out unfinished work.
items.reference:
Flag types
release toggle — hides unfinished work, temporary
ops/kill switch — instant production disable
experiment flag — A/B routing
permission toggle — plan/role gating, often long-term

Why: Different flag types have different expected lifespans — release toggles should be removed; permission toggles often shouldn't.

items.prompt: A flag gates a feature so only 'enterprise' plan customers can see it, and it's expected to stay in the code indefinitely. Which flag type is this?
choices: A permission toggle
A release toggle
An experiment flag
An ops toggle / kill switch
items.explanation: Permission toggles gate by plan or role and are often kept long-term, unlike release toggles which are meant to be removed once the feature fully ships.
items.reference:
Flag types
release toggle — hides unfinished work, temporary
ops/kill switch — instant production disable
experiment flag — A/B routing
permission toggle — plan/role gating, often long-term

Why: Different flag types have different expected lifespans — release toggles should be removed; permission toggles often shouldn't.

items.prompt: Why does separating 'merge' from 'release' help ship fast without breaking main?
choices: It lets code land in main constantly (cheap, reviewable) while exposure to real users happens on a separate, controllable schedule
It removes the need for a release process entirely
It means code never needs testing before merging
It makes git conflicts impossible
items.explanation: The whole benefit is that merging stops being gated on 'is this fully ready for every user' — that question moves to the flag, which can be answered gradually.
items.reference:
Merge vs. release
merging = a git event, safe and cheap
releasing = a business event, risky unless planned

Why: Once these are separate, small frequent merges no longer force premature, all-at-once releases.

items.prompt: Without feature flags, what forces 'finished' and 'merged' to become the same deadline?
choices: Because merging directly exposes the code to users, a PR can't merge until it's fully ready for everyone — so teams hold PRs open until 100% done
Git technically prevents merging incomplete code
Code review tools block partial features automatically
CI pipelines fail on unfinished features by default
items.explanation: When merge and release are the same event, a PR has to be fully production-ready before it can merge at all — this is exactly what balloons PRs into 9-day branches.
items.reference:
Merge vs. release
merging = a git event, safe and cheap
releasing = a business event, risky unless planned

Why: Once these are separate, small frequent merges no longer force premature, all-at-once releases.

items.prompt: According to this unit, what's the main risk of large pull requests?
choices: They take longer to review and stay open longer, letting main drift further away and conflicts accumulate
They always contain more bugs per line than small PRs
GitHub has a hard file-count limit that blocks large PRs
They cannot be merged with feature flags at all
items.explanation: Size itself isn't the direct danger — the time a large PR stays open while main keeps moving is what turns into growing conflicts, as in the 9-day scenario.
items.reference:
Small PRs
reviewable in minutes
less likely to drift into conflicts before merging

Why: The smaller and faster a PR merges, the less time main has to move away from it.

items.prompt: How do small PRs and trunk hygiene work together, per this unit's table?
choices: Small PRs keep changes reviewable and mergeable before main drifts far, which is what lets main stay in a hygienic, always-deployable state
They're unrelated practices with no connection to each other
Trunk hygiene requires disabling PR review entirely
Small PRs replace the need for feature flags completely
items.explanation: The three habits (small PRs, trunk hygiene, feature flags) reinforce each other — small PRs are specifically what keeps trunk hygiene achievable in practice.
items.reference:
Small PRs
reviewable in minutes
less likely to drift into conflicts before merging

Why: The smaller and faster a PR merges, the less time main has to move away from it.

items.prompt: Without feature flags, why do teams tend to let PRs balloon in size, per this unit?
choices: Because 'finished' and 'merged' become the same deadline, so developers hold off merging until the entire feature is done
Because git enforces a minimum PR size
Because reviewers prefer reviewing more code at once
Because CI only runs on PRs over a certain size
items.explanation: When there's no way to merge partial, hidden work safely, developers naturally wait to merge until the whole feature is ready — which is exactly what flags let them stop doing.
items.reference:
Small PRs
reviewable in minutes
less likely to drift into conflicts before merging

Why: The smaller and faster a PR merges, the less time main has to move away from it.

items.prompt: If everyone commits straight to main, where does 'in-progress, not-ready' code actually live?
choices: Inside the running code itself, gated by an if checking a flag — not in a separate git branch
In a special hidden git branch that only admins can see
It doesn't exist until the feature is fully done
In a separate, undeployed repository
items.explanation: Branch by abstraction moves the 'in progress' boundary from git (two divergent branches) into the code itself (one history, a runtime decision).
items.reference:
Branch by abstraction
one line of git history contains both old and new paths
a runtime if picks between them, not a git branch

Why: This is what makes trunk-based commits possible without exposing unfinished work.

items.prompt: In the pseudocode `if flags.isEnabled("new-checkout", user): return newCheckoutFlow(...) else: return oldCheckoutFlow(...)`, when can both functions be committed to main?
choices: Both can be committed, reviewed, and deployed in small pieces long before the flag ever flips to true for a real customer
Only oldCheckoutFlow can ever be in main; newCheckoutFlow must stay on a branch
Only after the flag is deleted
Never — one of the two functions must always be removed first
items.explanation: That's the entire point of branch by abstraction: both paths coexist safely in main, and only the flag's runtime evaluation decides which one actually runs.
items.reference:
Branch by abstraction
one line of git history contains both old and new paths
a runtime if picks between them, not a git branch

Why: This is what makes trunk-based commits possible without exposing unfinished work.

items.prompt: Why is a plain on/off boolean not enough for a flag gating something with real risk attached?
choices: It forces an all-or-nothing release, which recreates the same risk a giant PR has, just moved one step later
Booleans are technically impossible to store in most databases
It would require rewriting the entire codebase
Because JSON doesn't support boolean values
items.explanation: A flag that's only ever fully on or fully off can't gradually widen exposure — the risk of an all-at-once release just moves from deploy time to flag-flip time.
items.reference:
Targeting rules
userIdIn — always serve to specific users
percentageRollout — a widening slice
planTier — include/exclude by plan

Why: Rules are checked top to bottom; the first match wins.

items.prompt: In a flag config's rules array, in what order are rules evaluated?
choices: Top to bottom — the first rule that matches decides the result
Randomly, to keep evaluation unbiased
Bottom to top, always
All rules are evaluated and the majority result wins
items.explanation: Rules are an ordered program: evaluation stops at the first match, which is why rule order (e.g. an exclusion before or after a rollout rule) changes real behavior.
items.reference:
Targeting rules
userIdIn — always serve to specific users
percentageRollout — a widening slice
planTier — include/exclude by plan

Why: Rules are checked top to bottom; the first match wins.

items.prompt: In L2's example config, internal QA accounts see the new checkout flow before a 5% rollout begins. Why does that ordering matter?
choices: It ensures obvious bugs get caught by QA before any real customer is exposed to the new path at all
It has no effect — order in the rules array is cosmetic only
It's required by law for financial software
It makes the config file smaller
items.explanation: Putting the internal-only rule first guarantees QA always evaluates true before the percentage rule is even reached, catching problems before any paying customer sees the new path.
items.reference:
Targeting rules
userIdIn — always serve to specific users
percentageRollout — a widening slice
planTier — include/exclude by plan

Why: Rules are checked top to bottom; the first match wins.

items.prompt: A percentage rollout is set to 5%. Should the same user see the new flow on some page loads and the old flow on others?
choices: No — a well-built rollout is sticky per user, giving the same answer on every subsequent evaluation
Yes, that's expected and improves test coverage
Yes, but only on weekends
It depends entirely on the user's internet connection speed
items.explanation: The percentage decides who gets bucketed into the rollout once, typically via hashing a stable id, and that user gets the same result every time after that.
items.reference:
Sticky rollout
a user's bucket comes from hashing a stable id
same user -> same bucket -> same result, every time

Why: Without stickiness, a user could flip between old and new mid-session, corrupting a multi-step flow like checkout.

items.prompt: Why would a non-sticky (re-randomized per request) rollout be especially dangerous for a multi-step flow like checkout?
choices: A user could reach a later step using state built by a different flow than the one that rendered an earlier step, corrupting the process
It would only be a cosmetic UI flicker with no functional impact
Non-sticky rollouts are actually safer for multi-step flows
Checkout flows are not affected by feature flags at all
items.explanation: Flipping between old and new mid-session risks mismatched state between steps — e.g. cart data built one way, a confirmation screen expecting the other.
items.reference:
Sticky rollout
a user's bucket comes from hashing a stable id
same user -> same bucket -> same result, every time

Why: Without stickiness, a user could flip between old and new mid-session, corrupting a multi-step flow like checkout.

items.prompt: What typically makes a rollout sticky in practice?
choices: Hashing a stable identifier (like a user or account id) into a bucket, so the same input always produces the same bucket
Storing the user's choice in a cookie that expires after 5 minutes
Asking the user to manually opt in every time
Randomizing the result fresh on every single request
items.explanation: A deterministic hash of a stable id is what guarantees the same user always lands in the same bucket, which is the mechanism behind stickiness.
items.reference:
Sticky rollout
a user's bucket comes from hashing a stable id
same user -> same bucket -> same result, every time

Why: Without stickiness, a user could flip between old and new mid-session, corrupting a multi-step flow like checkout.

items.prompt: What is the internal-only rollout stage specifically checking for?
choices: Obvious bugs, before any real customer is exposed to the new path
Whether the code compiles at all
The exact final rollout percentage to use
Whether the flag system itself is working
items.explanation: Internal/dogfooding accounts see the new path first specifically to catch obvious problems before any real customer encounters them.
items.reference:
Rollout stages
0% -> internal only -> 5% -> 100%

Why: Each stage answers a narrower question than the last, from 'does it deploy' to 'is it fully ready to remove the flag'.

items.prompt: Once a rollout reaches 100%, per L2's lifecycle, is the flag's job done?
choices: Not quite — the flag still needs to be removed, along with the now-dead old code path, to avoid becoming flag debt
Yes, 100% means the flag can simply be forgotten with no further action
No, it needs to be reset back to 0% and rolled out again
Yes, but only for ops toggles, not release toggles
items.explanation: Reaching 100% is the second-to-last stage, not the last — cleanup (removing the flag and the dead path) is the step most often skipped and most important to do.
items.reference:
Rollout stages
0% -> internal only -> 5% -> 100%

Why: Each stage answers a narrower question than the last, from 'does it deploy' to 'is it fully ready to remove the flag'.

items.prompt: What is 'flag debt,' as this unit defines it?
choices: The accumulation of flags nobody remembers the purpose of, each one multiplying the code paths a future change could hit
Money a company owes for using a third-party flagging service
A specific git error caused by too many branches
The time it takes to originally implement a flag
items.explanation: Flag debt is specifically about unremoved flags accumulating and multiplying the paths through the code, not a cost related to the initial implementation.
items.reference:
Flag debt
each active flag doubles the code paths a change could hit
cleanup after 100% is what prevents this

Why: A flag at 100% for months isn't reducing risk anymore — it's pure complexity with none of the rollout benefit left.

items.prompt: Why does the unit call skipping cleanup a bigger problem than it sounds?
choices: Every active flag is a second code path future contributors must read, understand, and avoid breaking, for no remaining benefit once fully rolled out
Because unremoved flags cost extra money per flag per month in all cases
Because git refuses to merge new PRs while old flags exist
It isn't actually a problem — the unit says cleanup is optional
items.explanation: A flag left in after full rollout keeps the dead old path alive as ongoing cognitive load, with none of the gradual-rollout safety benefit remaining.
items.reference:
Flag debt
each active flag doubles the code paths a change could hit
cleanup after 100% is what prevents this

Why: A flag at 100% for months isn't reducing risk anymore — it's pure complexity with none of the rollout benefit left.

items.prompt: What's the fix the unit proposes for flag debt — banning flags?
choices: No — treating 'remove the flag and dead code' as part of the feature's definition of done, not an optional follow-up ticket
Yes, teams should stop using feature flags entirely
Limiting every team to exactly one active flag at a time
Automatically deleting all flags after 24 hours regardless of rollout status
items.explanation: The proposed fix is process, not prohibition — making cleanup part of 'done' is what keeps flags a net safety win instead of accumulating debt.
items.reference:
Flag debt
each active flag doubles the code paths a change could hit
cleanup after 100% is what prevents this

Why: A flag at 100% for months isn't reducing risk anymore — it's pure complexity with none of the rollout benefit left.

items.prompt: Implement `hashToBucket(key)` using FNV-1a hashing (offset basis 0x811c9dc5, prime 0x01000193, XOR each char code in then multiply with Math.imul, force unsigned with `>>> 0`, then `% 100`), matching this unit's L3. It must return the same number every time for the same key.
items.explanation: XOR-ing each character code into the running hash and multiplying by the FNV prime (via Math.imul for correct 32-bit overflow behavior) spreads the output roughly evenly; forcing unsigned with `>>> 0` before `% 100` guarantees a clean 0-99 range regardless of sign.
items.reference:
hashToBucket
same key -> same bucket, every call
0-99, roughly evenly spread

Why: Determinism is what makes a percentage rollout sticky per user instead of re-randomized per request.

items.prompt: Implement `hashToBucket(key)` (same FNV-1a algorithm as this unit's L3). Verify it against a different known key this time.

tests.description: a different key can land in a different bucket

items.explanation: Different keys scrambling to different buckets (here 9 vs 38) is what makes percentage rollout meaningfully split a population instead of grouping everyone together.
items.reference:
hashToBucket
same key -> same bucket, every call
0-99, roughly evenly spread

Why: Determinism is what makes a percentage rollout sticky per user instead of re-randomized per request.

items.prompt: Implement `hashToBucket(key)` (same FNV-1a algorithm as this unit's L3). This variant checks the salting property: the same user id combined with two different flag keys should not be forced into the same bucket.

tests.description: same user, different flag keys -> different buckets here

items.explanation: Salting the hash input with the flag's own key (not just the user id) is what stops the same lucky-bucket users from always being first into every rollout, flag after flag.
items.reference:
hashToBucket
same key -> same bucket, every call
0-99, roughly evenly spread

Why: Determinism is what makes a percentage rollout sticky per user instead of re-randomized per request.

tests.description: kill switch overrides an otherwise-matching 100% rollout
tests.expr: expect(evaluateFlag({ key: "new-checkout", default: false, killSwitch: true, rules: [{ type: "percentageRollout", percent: 100, serve: true }] }, { userId: "user-1", planTier: "standard" })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "kill-switch" })

items.explanation: Checking `killSwitch` before any rule loop is what lets ops disable a feature for 100% of traffic with one config flip, with no rule evaluation able to override it — exactly the Day 3 incident in L3.
items.reference:
evaluateFlag
killSwitch overrides everything, unconditionally
rules checked in order, first match wins
falls back to config.default if nothing matches

Why: This one function is what turns a config into a single enabled/disabled decision per request.

tests.description: listed user always matches userIdIn first
tests.expr: expect(evaluateFlag({ key: "new-checkout", default: false, killSwitch: false, rules: [{ type: "userIdIn", values: ["internal-qa-1"], serve: true }, { type: "percentageRollout", percent: 20, serve: true }] }, { userId: "internal-qa-1", planTier: "standard" })).toEqual({ enabled: true, reason: "userIdIn" })

tests.description: non-listed user falls through to percentageRollout and matches (bucket 15 < 20)
tests.expr: expect(evaluateFlag({ key: "new-checkout", default: false, killSwitch: false, rules: [{ type: "userIdIn", values: ["internal-qa-1"], serve: true }, { type: "percentageRollout", percent: 20, serve: true }] }, { userId: "user-100", planTier: "standard" })).toEqual({ enabled: true, reason: "percentageRollout" })

tests.description: a user outside both rules falls back to default (bucket 26 >= 20)
tests.expr: expect(evaluateFlag({ key: "new-checkout", default: false, killSwitch: false, rules: [{ type: "userIdIn", values: ["internal-qa-1"], serve: true }, { type: "percentageRollout", percent: 20, serve: true }] }, { userId: "user-42", planTier: "standard" })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "default" })

items.explanation: Rules are an ordered program: the loop returns on the first match, so a `userIdIn` rule placed before `percentageRollout` always wins for listed users, and everyone else falls through to the percentage check, then the default.
items.reference:
evaluateFlag
killSwitch overrides everything, unconditionally
rules checked in order, first match wins
falls back to config.default if nothing matches

Why: This one function is what turns a config into a single enabled/disabled decision per request.

tests.description: enterprise plan is excluded even though default is true
tests.expr: expect(evaluateFlag({ key: "new-checkout", default: true, killSwitch: false, rules: [{ type: "planTier", values: ["enterprise"], serve: false }] }, { userId: "user-1", planTier: "enterprise" })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "planTier" })

tests.description: a standard-plan user falls through to the true default
tests.expr: expect(evaluateFlag({ key: "new-checkout", default: true, killSwitch: false, rules: [{ type: "planTier", values: ["enterprise"], serve: false }] }, { userId: "user-1", planTier: "standard" })).toEqual({ enabled: true, reason: "default" })

items.explanation: A rule doesn't have to mean 'turn this on' — `serve: false` lets a rule carve out an exclusion even when the flag otherwise defaults to true for everyone else.
items.reference:
evaluateFlag
killSwitch overrides everything, unconditionally
rules checked in order, first match wins
falls back to config.default if nothing matches

Why: This one function is what turns a config into a single enabled/disabled decision per request.

items.prompt: If two different flags both use a 5% rollout, and a user is in the first flag's 5%, should you expect them to also be in the second flag's 5%?
choices: Not more than random chance predicts — the bucket key combines the flag's own key with the user id, scrambling the result independently per flag
Yes, always — the same users are permanently in every rollout's lucky percentage
No, it's mathematically impossible for the same user to ever be in two rollouts
Only if both flags were created on the same day
items.explanation: Salting the hash input with the flag's key (not the user id alone) means being in one flag's 5% carries no information about another flag's 5% — each flag scrambles independently.
items.reference:
Salting the bucket key
bucket key = `${flagKey}:${userId}`, not just userId

Why: Without the flag key mixed in, the same 'lucky' users would land in every flag's rollout percentage, every time.

items.prompt: What would go wrong if `hashToBucket` were called with just the user id, with no flag key mixed in?
choices: The same subset of users would always be selected first for every rollout ever created, across the whole product
The hash function would throw an error and crash
Nothing — the flag key is purely cosmetic and has no effect on bucketing
Rollout percentages would always come out as exactly 50%
items.explanation: Without salting per flag, a user's bucket would be fixed once, globally — meaning the earliest-bucketed users would be first into every single rollout forever, defeating independent random sampling.
items.reference:
Salting the bucket key
bucket key = `${flagKey}:${userId}`, not just userId

Why: Without the flag key mixed in, the same 'lucky' users would land in every flag's rollout percentage, every time.

items.prompt: Per L3's worked example, what does flipping `killSwitch: true` require operationally?
choices: Nothing beyond an ops dashboard config change — no redeploy and no git operation at all
A full CI/CD pipeline run followed by a production deploy
Opening a new pull request and getting it reviewed first
Reverting the most recent git commit on main
items.explanation: The kill switch is just a stored config field; `evaluateFlag` checks it first on every call, so the very next evaluation reflects the change with no deploy step involved.
items.reference:
Kill switch
one config field flip -> enabled: false for everyone, instantly
no deploy, no git operation required

Why: This is what turned Day 3's error spike into a five-minute non-event instead of an outage.

items.prompt: Once `killSwitch` is true, can a `userIdIn` rule that would otherwise match still enable the flag for that user?
choices: No — the kill switch check happens first and returns immediately, before any rule in the array is even considered
Yes, userIdIn rules always take priority over the kill switch
Only if the user is on the enterprise plan
It depends on the order of the rules array
items.explanation: `evaluateFlag` returns on the kill switch check before the rules loop ever runs, so no rule — regardless of type or position — can override it.
items.reference:
Kill switch
one config field flip -> enabled: false for everyone, instantly
no deploy, no git operation required

Why: This is what turned Day 3's error spike into a five-minute non-event instead of an outage.

items.prompt: Implement `countPathCombinations(activeFlagCount)`, matching L3's table: the number of distinct code-path combinations grows as 2 raised to the number of simultaneously active flags.
items.explanation: Each flag independently doubles the space of possible combinations (on/off for each), which is exactly why 2**n — not n — is the honest cost of leaving flags active indefinitely.

Flag debt cost
each active flag doubles the possible code paths
1 flag=2, 3 flags=8, 6 flags=64

Why: This growth is why leaving a fully-rolled-out flag in place has a real, compounding cost.

1 flag=2, 3 flags=8, 6 flags=64

items.prompt: L3's extend-it-yourself question asks how to offer the new checkout first to enterprise beta users, falling back to random rollout for everyone else. What change accomplishes this?
choices: Move a `planTier` rule with `serve: true` ahead of the percentage rule, so enterprise beta users match and return early before the percentage check runs
Delete the percentage rollout rule entirely and only use planTier
Set `killSwitch: true` for enterprise accounts specifically
Rename the flag's key to include the word 'enterprise'
items.explanation: Because rules are checked in order with the first match winning, placing a serve:true planTier rule ahead of the percentage rule guarantees enterprise beta users match immediately, without changing evaluateFlag's logic at all.
items.reference:
Rule order changes behavior
rules are a small ordered program
moving a rule earlier, or flipping its serve value, changes who matches first

Why: Reordering or flipping one rule can redirect an entire rollout without touching evaluateFlag itself.

items.prompt: In L2's original config, a `planTier` rule excludes enterprise accounts (`serve: false`) and sits after the percentage rule. What's different about the extend-it-yourself version's planTier rule?
choices: It moves earlier in the array and flips to `serve: true`, turning an exclusion into a priority inclusion
It's identical — no change is actually needed to offer enterprise users the new flow first
It becomes a killSwitch rule instead of a planTier rule
It's removed entirely and replaced with a userIdIn rule
items.explanation: The same rule type (planTier) can express opposite intents purely through its position and `serve` value — later and false to exclude, earlier and true to prioritize — with no new rule type needed.
items.reference:
Rule order changes behavior
rules are a small ordered program
moving a rule earlier, or flipping its serve value, changes who matches first

Why: Reordering or flipping one rule can redirect an entire rollout without touching evaluateFlag itself.
